newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Wages help Australia bonds, Greenspan a worry.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Wages help Australia bonds, Greenspan a worry.

text.p: *Australian bonds yields ended well below their after hours highs helped by short position profit-taking and further signs of moderating wages growth.
*Market wary of further fall out from Greenspan comments.

Further signs of moderating wages growth helped the Australian bond market recover a large proportion of its huge after hours sell-off, but the market will remain wary of any further fall out in U.S. markets.

Local long-dated yields had spiked to their highest level this year as U.S. Treasuries and stocks came under intense pressure following hawkish comments by Federal Reserve Alan Greenspan at his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday.
But profit-taking on short positions and today's data, which also covered capital expenditure, prompted a partial recovery.
Final average weekly earnings data for the November quarter showed private sector wages growth rising just 0.8 percent to 2.8 percent year-on-year.

"One more potential threat to inflation has been averted, so these data are market friendly, though they scarely offset the trepidation caused by Dr Greenspan's ruminations," said Chris Caton, chief economist at Bankers Trust Australia.
U.S. markets were sent reeling after Greenspan warned that U.S. stocks had risen too far, that there are inflation risks to the upside and that he could not rule out a pre-emptive tightening.

Matthew Drennan, senior economist at Axiom Funds management, said local debt markets were oversold on Greenspan comments noting that the had priced in a 40 basis point tightening in policy by September.

"Given Australia's benign outlook for inflation over 1997 the reaction was too extreme and today's capex numbers brought this back into focus. Longer term, though, economic fundamentals confirm that the risks are for higher yields as we move through 1997," Drennan said.
New capital expenditure fell 2.4 percent in the December quarter when forecasts had centred on a 2.1 percent rise.

But, looking ahead, Drennan noted that the first estimate for capital expenditure for 1997/98 contained in today's data suggested an increase of 10.1 percent, while residential building is turning up and employment growth had quickened.
Meanwhile, while U.S. analysts expect a calmer session in U.S. Treasuries on Thursday, the market does face January durable goods orders later today.
There will also obviously be some concerns over what the Fed Chairman might say when he returns to the podium to give the second half of his testimony on March 5.

The local market's partial rebound saw spreads tighten to the U.S. and Canada, particularly at the short-end of the curve. The contraction was less pronounced against New Zealand, which responded to a fairly positive outcome to its N.Z. Treasury bond tender.
